## Hamiltonian Mechanics

**Hamiltonian mechanics** reformulates [[lagrangian-mechanics]] in terms of
positions $\boldsymbol{q}$ and momenta $\boldsymbol{p}$, replacing the $n$
second-order Euler-Lagrange equations by $2n$ first-order equations. It is
equivalent to Newton's laws and to the Lagrangian formulation, and is the
natural setting for conservation laws and the
[[hamilton-jacobi-equation]].

Let $\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{q},\dot{\boldsymbol{q}},t)$ be the
[[lagrangian-mechanics|Lagrangian]] of a system with generalised coordinates
$\boldsymbol{q}=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$. The **momenta** are
$$
p_{i}:=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot q_{i}}.
$$

:::{.definition data-title="Hamiltonian"}

Assume the map $\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}\mapsto\boldsymbol{p}$ is invertible. The
**Hamiltonian** is the Legendre transform of $\mathcal{L}$ in the velocities,
$$
H(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{p},t)=\sum_{i=1}^np_i\dot q_i-\mathcal{L}
(\boldsymbol{q},\dot{\boldsymbol{q}},t),
$$
with $\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}$ expressed as a function of
$(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{p},t)$. The space of pairs
$(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{p})$ is the **phase space**.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Hamilton's Equations"}

The Euler-Lagrange equations are equivalent to
$$
\dot q_i=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i},\qquad
\dot p_i=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i},\qquad
\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial t}.
$$
Moreover, along solutions $\dfrac{dH}{dt}=\dfrac{\partial H}{\partial t}$, so
$H$ is conserved when the system has no explicit time dependence.

:::

:::{.proof}

Differentiating $H=\sum p_i\dot q_i-\mathcal{L}$ with respect to $q_i$ at fixed
$p$, the terms involving $\partial\dot q/\partial q_i$ cancel because
$p_j=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot q_j$:
$$
\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}=-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i}
=-\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot q_i}=-\dot p_i,
$$
using the Euler-Lagrange equation. The same cancellation gives
$\partial H/\partial p_i=\dot q_i$ and $\partial H/\partial t=-\partial
\mathcal{L}/\partial t$. Finally
$$
\frac{dH}{dt}=\sum_i\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}\dot q_i
+\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\dot p_i\right)+\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}
=\frac{\partial H}{\partial t},
$$
since the bracket is $-\dot p_i\dot q_i+\dot q_i\dot p_i=0$.

:::

For $\mathcal{L}=K-U$ with kinetic energy quadratic in the velocities, $H=K+U$
is the total energy.

:::{.example data-title="Pendulum"}

For the pendulum with $\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12ml^2\dot\theta^2+mgl\cos\theta$ we
have $p=ml^2\dot\theta$ and
$$
H=p\dot\theta-\mathcal{L}=\frac{p^2}{2ml^2}-mgl\cos\theta.
$$
Hamilton's equations are $\dot\theta=p/(ml^2)$ and $\dot p=-mgl\sin\theta$,
which combine to $\ddot\theta=-(g/l)\sin\theta$. Since $H$ does not depend on
$t$, the energy $H$ is conserved and the orbits in phase space are its level
sets.

:::

## Hamiltonian Matrices

For a system with a quadratic Hamiltonian $H=\tfrac12\boldsymbol{z}^\top S
\boldsymbol{z}$ in $\boldsymbol{z}=(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{p})$, with $S$
symmetric, Hamilton's equations are linear, $\dot{\boldsymbol{z}}=JS
\boldsymbol{z}$, where
$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}0_{n}&I_{n}\\-I_{n}&0_{n}\end{bmatrix}
$$
is skew-symmetric and $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity. This motivates:

:::{.definition data-title="Hamiltonian Matrix"}

A $2n\times2n$ matrix $A$ is a **Hamiltonian matrix** if $JA$ is symmetric,
equivalently $JA+A^\top J=0$.

:::

The matrix $A=JS$ is Hamiltonian since $JA=J^2S=-S$ is symmetric.

:::{.proposition data-title="Spectrum of a Hamiltonian Matrix"}

If $A$ is Hamiltonian then $A^\top=JAJ$, so $A$ is similar to $-A^\top$. Hence
the eigenvalues of $A$ come in pairs $\{\lambda,-\lambda\}$.

:::

:::{.proof}

From $JA+A^\top J=0$ and $J^{-1}=-J$ we get
$A^\top=-JAJ^{-1}=JAJ$, hence $-A^\top=JAJ^{-1}$, so $A$ is similar to
$-A^\top$. Similar matrices share eigenvalues, and $A^\top$ has the same
eigenvalues as $A$, so the spectrum of $A$ equals its negative.

:::

In particular a linear Hamiltonian system cannot be asymptotically stable.

## The Control Hamiltonian

In [[control-theory]] the word **Hamiltonian** refers to a function that
encodes both the **dynamics** and the **objective** of an
optimal control problem. It is the instantaneous increment of the
[[lagrange-multiplier-method|Lagrangian]] of the problem, and the structure is
the same as in mechanics: the state $\boldsymbol{x}$ plays the role of
$\boldsymbol{q}$, the costate $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ the role of
$\boldsymbol{p}$.

### Control Problem

The system has dynamics given by $n$
[[ordinary-differential-equations|first-order ODEs]]
$$
\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}(t)=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}(t),\boldsymbol{u}(t),t),
\qquad \boldsymbol{x}(t_0)=\boldsymbol{x}_0,
$$
where $\boldsymbol{x}(t)\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is the **state
vector** and $\boldsymbol{u}(t)\in\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^r$ is the
**control vector**, with $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U}$ the admissible sets. For
given $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ and control the solution is a **trajectory**. The
problem is to choose $\boldsymbol{u}$ to minimise the **cost functional**
$$
J(\boldsymbol{u})=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}L(\boldsymbol{x}(t),\boldsymbol{u}(t),t)
~dt+\phi(\boldsymbol{x}(t_{1})),
$$
where $L$ is the **running cost** and $\phi$ the **terminal cost**, subject to
the dynamics above.

:::{.definition data-title="Control Hamiltonian"}

The **control Hamiltonian** is
$$
H(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{\lambda},t)
=L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u},t)
+\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\top}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u},t),
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\lambda}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is the **costate** (or
**adjoint**) vector.

:::

This combines the objective and the state equations as in a static
[[lagrange-multiplier-method|Lagrangian]], except that the multipliers
$\boldsymbol{\lambda}(t)$ are functions of time rather than constants.

:::{.intuition data-title="Cost now versus cost later"}

The Hamiltonian combines the **instantaneous cost**, via $L$, and the
**effect of the control on the future**, via $\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top
\boldsymbol{f}$. We want a control that not only keeps the immediate cost low
but also drives the system in a direction favourable in the long run, as
measured by the costate.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Pontryagin Maximum Principle"}

An optimal pair $(\boldsymbol{x}^*,\boldsymbol{u}^*)$ satisfies, for some
costate $\boldsymbol{\lambda}(t)$:

- **State equation** (forward in time from $\boldsymbol{x}(t_0)$):
  $$\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
  =\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u},t).$$
- **Adjoint equation** (backward in time from the terminal condition):
  $$\dot{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}},
  \qquad\boldsymbol{\lambda}(t_{1})=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial
  \boldsymbol{x}}(\boldsymbol{x}(t_{1})).$$
- **Optimality condition:** the optimal control minimises the Hamiltonian,
  $$\boldsymbol{u}^*(t)=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{u}\in\mathcal{U}}
  H(\boldsymbol{x}^*(t),\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{\lambda}(t),t).$$
  For an unconstrained interior solution this reduces to
  $\partial H/\partial\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{0}$. For maximisation
  problems $\arg\min$ becomes $\arg\max$.

:::

Since $\boldsymbol{x}$ has a condition at $t_0$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ at
$t_1$, this is a **two-point boundary value problem**. The state and adjoint
equations are exactly Hamilton's equations for $H$.

### Example: Linear-Quadratic Regulator

:::{.example data-title="Scalar LQR"}

Take dynamics $\dot x=ax+bu$ and cost
$J(u)=\int_0^T\left(\tfrac12qx^2+\tfrac12ru^2\right)dt$ with $q\ge0$, $r>0$
and no terminal cost.

**Hamiltonian.** With scalar costate $\lambda$,
$H=\tfrac12qx^2+\tfrac12ru^2+\lambda(ax+bu)$.

**Optimal control.** $\partial H/\partial u=ru+\lambda b=0$, so
$u^*=-\dfrac{b}{r}\lambda$.

**State and adjoint equations.**
$$
\dot x=ax-\frac{b^2}{r}\lambda,\qquad
\dot\lambda=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}=-qx-a\lambda,\quad\lambda(T)=0.
$$
In the variable $(x,\lambda)$ this linear system has matrix
$\begin{bmatrix}a&-b^2/r\\-q&-a\end{bmatrix}$, which is a Hamiltonian matrix.

**Riccati equation.** Posing $\lambda(t)=P(t)x(t)$ and substituting into the
adjoint equation gives
$$
-\dot P=2aP-\frac{b^2}{r}P^2+q,\qquad P(T)=0,
$$
and the optimal control takes the feedback form $u^*=-\dfrac{b}{r}P(t)x(t)$.

:::
